title: Math is Ingenuity
contentObjective: I can use ratios and models to explain how the Penny Farthing and gear-driven bicycles were ingenious solutions to a real problem.
languageObjective: I can explain a gear ratio using the words rotation, teeth, and 'for each ___, the wheel turns ___.'

turnAndTalk.question: The Penny Farthing's pedals are attached directly to the front wheel — a 1 to 1 ratio. Why did inventors make the front wheel so large?
turnAndTalk.kernel: One pedal rotation makes one wheel rotation, so a bigger wheel's longer perimeter carries the bicycle farther with each pedal push.

stems.en: The front wheel is large because it ___ the distance traveled per pedal rotation.
stems.es: La rueda delantera es grande porque ___ la distancia recorrida por cada rotación del pedal.
La razón entre el pedal y la rueda es ___ a ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: A strong answer connects the 1-to-1 ratio to the wheel's perimeter, explaining a bigger wheel travels farther per pedal push. A weak answer just says 'bigger is faster' without naming the ratio or perimeter.
turnAndTalk.extend: If the front wheel had been smaller, how would the 1-to-1 pedal ratio change, and how would the bicycle's distance per pedal rotation change?
extendStems: The ratio would stay ___, but the distance per rotation would ___ because ___.
This shows the ratio and the distance are ___ things.

turnAndTalk.question: When you sorted facts about the 32-tooth gear and the 12-tooth gear, why does the SMALLER gear give MORE wheel rotations per pedal rotation?
turnAndTalk.kernel: 48 ÷ 32 = 1.5 rotations, but 48 ÷ 12 = 4 rotations — a smaller gear needs fewer teeth to complete a rotation, so it spins more times per pedal push.

stems.en: The 12-tooth gear gives more rotations because ___.
stems.es: El engranaje de 12 dientes da más rotaciones porque ___.

stems.en: The 32-tooth gear gives fewer rotations because ___.
stems.es: El engranaje de 32 dientes da menos rotaciones porque ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Listen for students explaining that fewer teeth means the gear completes a full turn sooner (48 ÷ 12 = 4), not just repeating 'smaller is faster' without the division.
turnAndTalk.extend: A student claims 'more teeth always means more rotations.' Use the 48-tooth pedal gear and either rear gear to argue against that claim.
extendStems: The 32-tooth gear actually gives ___ rotations, which is ___ than the 12-tooth gear's ___ rotations.

turnAndTalk.question: A future vehicle's motor gear has 40 teeth turning a wheel gear with 10 teeth. Using the same math as the bicycle's chain, how many wheel rotations happen per motor rotation?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Dividing the motor gear's teeth by the wheel gear's teeth gives the ratio: 40 ÷ 10 = 4 wheel rotations per motor rotation.

stems.en: The wheel makes ___ rotations per motor rotation because 40 ÷ ___ = ___.
stems.es: La rueda hace ___ rotaciones por cada rotación del motor porque 40 ÷ ___ = ___.

stems.en: This is the same math as the bicycle because both ___.
stems.es: Esto es la misma matemática que la bicicleta porque ambos ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: A strong answer divides 40 ÷ 10 = 4 correctly and names the same division-of-teeth structure as the bicycle's 48 ÷ 32 and 48 ÷ 12. A weak answer just says 'gears turn' with no ratio.
turnAndTalk.extend: Design a gear pair for a future vehicle where the wheel makes exactly 5 rotations per motor rotation, if the motor gear has 40 teeth. What must the wheel gear's tooth count be, and how do you know?
extendStems: The wheel gear needs ___ teeth because 40 ÷ ___ = 5.

turnAndTalk.question: During practice, when a problem gave you two gear tooth counts, what strategy helped you find the rotation ratio?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Dividing the pedal gear's teeth by the rear gear's teeth gives the number of wheel rotations per pedal rotation.

stems.en: I found the ratio by ___ the pedal gear's teeth by the rear gear's teeth.
stems.es: Encontré la razón al ___ los dientes del engranaje del pedal entre los dientes del engranaje trasero.

stems.en: I knew my answer was reasonable because ___.
stems.es: Supe que mi respuesta era razonable porque ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Listen for students naming division of tooth counts as the specific strategy, not just "I did math with the numbers."

launch.narrative: The invention of the bicycle in the late 1800s offered people a way to move about easily. Among the first bicycles created was the Penny Farthing, with a large front wheel and a small rear wheel. Ingenuity in mathematics helps us come up with different, and sometimes unique, solutions to problems.

conceptIntro.heading: Math can power ingenious solutions
conceptIntro.intro: The Penny Farthing is powered by the rider: pushing the pedals rotates the front wheel directly, so each pedal rotation rotates the wheel one time — a 1 to 1 ratio.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: With each pedal rotation, the bicycle travels the length of the perimeter of the wheel. The front wheel is large so the bicycle travels a greater distance with one pedal rotation.

iDo.title: Watch me use a gear ratio
lines: A later bicycle design uses a chain: the pedal gear has 48 teeth, and the largest rear gear has 32 teeth.
For each rotation of the 48-tooth pedal gear, the wheel gear also turns 48 teeth.
The 32-tooth gear needs to turn 32 teeth to make one full rotation, so I find the equivalent ratio: 48 ÷ 32 = 1.5.
The rear wheel makes 1.5 rotations for each pedal rotation — this gear makes it easier to pedal at slower speeds or go uphill.

weDo.title: Let's do the smallest gear together
lines: The smallest rear gear has 12 teeth, and the pedal gear still turns 48 teeth per rotation.
One full rotation of the 12-tooth gear takes 12 teeth.
48 ÷ 12 = 4, so the rear wheel makes 4 rotations for each pedal rotation.
This gear makes it easier to pedal at faster speeds or go downhill.

youDo.title: Now you try
lines: Explain to a partner why the Penny Farthing's front wheel was so large.
Then say which rear gear — 32 teeth or 12 teeth — you would choose for a steep hill, and why.

explore.label: Which rear gear does each fact describe? Sort them.

explore.instructions: Both gears use the same 48-tooth pedal gear — the difference is how many teeth the rear gear needs to make one full rotation. After sorting, tell a partner what you notice about gear size and the distance the bike travels.

diagram.title: Gear Ratio: 40 Teeth to 10 Teeth
diagram.caption: The 40-tooth motor gear is 4 copies of the 10-tooth wheel gear, so 40 ÷ 10 = 4 and the wheel turns 4 times for every 1 turn of the motor gear.

connect.scenario: Humans have long looked for ways to travel easily and quickly. One modern option is a motorized unicycle. Imagine what a future mode of individual transportation might look like.
connect.promptQuestion: How will your future vehicle be powered, and what math will be used in its design or use?
connect.prompt: Describe a future mode of individual transportation. A complete answer says how it is ___, names a ___ (or rate) that shapes it, and explains where that math appears in the vehicle's ___.

check.stem: A future vehicle's design uses a motor gear with 40 teeth turning a wheel gear with 10 teeth. Following the gear-ratio math from this lesson, how many wheel rotations happen for each motor gear rotation?
check.explanation: 40 ÷ 10 = 4, the same way the bicycle's 48-tooth pedal gear was divided by the rear gear's teeth. 0.25 divides the wrong way around, 30 subtracts instead of dividing, and 400 multiplies instead of dividing.

check.stem: Why does a complete connect answer need to name a specific piece of math instead of just saying 'it uses math'?
choices: Naming the actual ratio, measurement, or rate shows the math really shaped the design, not just that math exists somewhere
Because grading requires exactly one number in every answer
Because the word 'math' cannot be used in a written answer
Because a vehicle description never needs any math at all
check.explanation: The lesson's check criteria call for pointing to specific math in the design — a vague claim that 'it uses math' does not show which math or how it mattered, the same way saying a bicycle 'uses gears' does not explain the 48-to-32 ratio.

check.stem: A student's answer says only, 'My vehicle is powered by a battery.' Which addition would make this a complete connect answer, based on this lesson's check?
choices: Naming a specific ratio or rate in the design, like a gear ratio between a motor and a wheel
Saying the vehicle looks very futuristic
Saying the vehicle is extremely fast
Repeating that it is powered by a battery a second time
check.explanation: Naming the power source alone is only one part of a complete answer — the check also requires pointing to specific math in the design, such as a gear ratio, measurement, or rate.

connect.modelAnswer: My vehicle is a one-wheeled electric scooter powered by a battery and the rider's balance. Its design uses a gear ratio between the motor and the wheel: if the motor gear turns 4 times for each wheel rotation, the designers can trade speed for climbing power, just like the bicycle gears with 48, 32, and 12 teeth.

approaching.stem: On the Penny Farthing, what is the ratio of pedal rotations to front-wheel rotations?
approaching.explanation: The pedals are attached directly to the front wheel, so each pedal rotation rotates the wheel one time — a 1 to 1 ratio.
choiceFeedback: 1 to 2 would mean each pedal rotation turns the wheel twice, but the pedals are attached directly to the wheel.
2 to 1 would mean the rider must pedal twice for one wheel turn, but one pedal rotation gives one wheel rotation.
1 to 4 describes the chain bike's smallest gear, not the Penny Farthing.
hints: The pedals are attached directly to the front wheel.
One pedal rotation makes the wheel turn how many times?
Each pedal rotation rotates the wheel one time.

approaching.stem: How far does the Penny Farthing travel with each pedal rotation?
choices: The length of the perimeter of the front wheel
It does not move a fixed distance
approaching.explanation: One wheel rotation rolls the bike forward exactly the perimeter of the wheel, and one pedal rotation makes one wheel rotation.
choiceFeedback: The rider's height does not determine rolling distance — the wheel's perimeter does.
The pedal's length changes how hard you have to push, not how far the wheel rolls in one turn.
It does move a fixed distance — one full roll of the wheel is always the same length.
hints: Picture the wheel rolling one full turn on the ground.
The distance it covers is the distance all the way around the wheel.
That distance around the wheel is its perimeter.

approaching.stem: Why was the front wheel of the Penny Farthing so large?
choices: So the bicycle travels a greater distance with one pedal rotation
So the bicycle is easier to stop
So the rider sits closer to the ground
So the rear wheel spins faster
approaching.explanation: A bigger wheel has a longer perimeter, so each pedal rotation carries the rider farther.
choiceFeedback: A huge front wheel actually made the Penny Farthing harder, not easier, to stop.
The large wheel puts the rider high UP, not close to the ground.
The rear wheel is not pedaled at all — the front wheel does the work.
hints: Each pedal rotation moves the bike one perimeter of the wheel.
Compare the perimeter of a big wheel and a small wheel.
A bigger wheel means a longer distance per pedal rotation.

approaching.stem: How does the size of the front wheel affect the distance the bicycle travels?
approaching.modelAnswer: The bigger the front wheel, the longer its perimeter, so one pedal rotation carries the bicycle a greater distance. A smaller front wheel would travel a shorter distance with each pedal rotation.
sentenceStems: A bigger wheel travels ___ with each pedal rotation because ___ .

approaching.stem: For each rotation of the 48-tooth pedal gear, how many teeth does the wheel gear turn?
approaching.explanation: The chain links the gears, so one full rotation of the 48-tooth pedal gear pulls 48 teeth of chain past the wheel gear.
choiceFeedback: 32 is the tooth count of the largest rear gear, not the number of teeth the chain moves.
12 is the tooth count of the smallest rear gear, not the number of teeth the chain moves.
One rotation moves every tooth on the pedal gear past the chain, not just one.
hints: The chain moves one link for each tooth on the pedal gear.
Read the tooth count printed on the pedal gear in the question.
Count the teeth the chain pulls in one full turn of the pedal gear — that is how many the wheel gear turns.

approaching.stem: Name one ingenious solution — from this lesson or from your own life — where math helped solve an everyday problem.
approaching.modelAnswer: The Penny Farthing's inventors used math: they knew a bigger wheel has a longer perimeter, so making the front wheel huge let riders travel farther with each pedal push.

onLevel.stem: The pedal gear turns 48 teeth per rotation. The largest rear gear needs 32 teeth for one full rotation. How many rotations does the rear wheel make for each pedal rotation?
onLevel.explanation: 48 ÷ 32 = 1.5, so the rear wheel makes 1.5 rotations for each pedal rotation.
choiceFeedback: That subtracts 48 − 32 instead of dividing 48 by 32.
That divides 32 by 48 the wrong way around — the wheel turns MORE than once, not less.
2 rotations would need a 24-tooth gear, since 48 ÷ 24 = 2.
hints: The chain delivers 48 teeth of motion; the gear uses 32 per rotation.
How many groups of 32 fit in 48?
Divide 48 by 32.

onLevel.stem: The smallest rear gear has 12 teeth. How many rotations will the rear wheel make for each rotation of the 48-tooth pedal gear?
onLevel.explanation: 48 ÷ 12 = 4, so the rear wheel makes 4 rotations for each pedal rotation.
choiceFeedback: That subtracts 48 − 12 instead of dividing 48 by 12.
3 rotations would need a 16-tooth gear, since 48 ÷ 16 = 3.
That divides 12 by 48 the wrong way around — the small gear turns MORE than the pedal gear, not less.
hints: The chain delivers 48 teeth of motion; this gear uses only 12 per rotation.
How many groups of 12 fit in 48?
Divide 48 by 12.

onLevel.stem: You are about to ride up a steep hill. Which rear gear should the chain be on, and why?
choices: The 32-tooth gear, because 1.5 rotations per pedal makes pedaling easier at slow speeds
The 12-tooth gear, because 4 rotations per pedal is always better
The 32-tooth gear, because it makes the bike go faster
It does not matter which gear you use on a hill
onLevel.explanation: The larger gear turns the wheel fewer times per pedal rotation, which makes it easier to pedal at slower speeds or go uphill.
choiceFeedback: The 12-tooth gear is for speed on flat ground or downhill — on a hill it makes each pedal push much harder.
The 32-tooth gear is the slower gear, not the faster one; its advantage on a hill is easier pedaling.
It matters a great deal — that is the whole point of having gears of different sizes.
hints: Uphill, you want each pedal push to be easier, not faster.
Which gear gives FEWER wheel rotations per pedal rotation?
The larger gear: 48 ÷ 32 = 1.5 rotations.

onLevel.stem: Why do you think the larger gear makes it easier to pedal at slower speeds?
onLevel.modelAnswer: With the larger gear the rear wheel only makes 1.5 rotations per pedal rotation instead of 4, so each pedal push moves the bike a shorter distance. Moving a shorter distance per push takes less force, which is easier when going slowly or uphill.
sentenceStems: With the larger gear, each pedal rotation only turns the wheel ___ .

onLevel.stem: With the chain on the 12-tooth gear, the rider makes 10 pedal rotations. How many rotations does the rear wheel make?
onLevel.explanation: The rear wheel makes 4 rotations per pedal rotation, so 10 pedal rotations give 10 × 4 = 40 wheel rotations.
choiceFeedback: That adds 10 + 4 instead of multiplying.
That adds 10 + 12 instead of using the 4-rotations-per-pedal ratio.
That multiplies 10 by the 12 teeth instead of by the 4 rotations per pedal rotation.
hints: First find the rotations per single pedal rotation: 48 ÷ 12.
That is 4 wheel rotations for each pedal rotation.
Now scale up: 10 pedal rotations × 4.

onLevel.stem: When the chain is on the largest gear the rear wheel makes 1.5 rotations per pedal rotation; on the smallest gear it makes 4. What do you notice about the size of the wheel gears and the distance the bike travels?
onLevel.modelAnswer: The smaller the rear gear, the more rotations the wheel makes per pedal rotation, so the bike travels farther with each pedal push. The larger gear gives fewer rotations and a shorter distance, but easier pedaling.
sentenceStems: As the rear gear gets smaller, the wheel makes ___ rotations, so the bike travels ___ .

extending.stem: The rider makes 3 full pedal rotations with the chain on the 32-tooth gear. How many rotations does the rear wheel make?
extending.explanation: Three pedal rotations move 3 × 48 = 144 teeth of chain, and 144 ÷ 32 = 4.5 rear-wheel rotations.
choiceFeedback: 3 rotations forgets the gear ratio — the wheel turns 1.5 times for EACH pedal rotation, not once.
96 is 3 × 32, which multiplies by the gear's teeth instead of finding rotations.
6 uses a ratio of 2 rotations per pedal, but 48 ÷ 32 = 1.5, not 2.
hints: Each pedal rotation gives 48 ÷ 32 = 1.5 wheel rotations.
You have 3 pedal rotations.
Multiply 3 × 1.5.

extending.stem: A designer adds a middle gear so the rear wheel makes exactly 2 rotations per rotation of the 48-tooth pedal gear. How many teeth must the new gear have?
extending.explanation: The gear must use 48 ÷ 2 = 24 teeth per rotation, so a 24-tooth gear gives exactly 2 rotations.
choiceFeedback: 48 ÷ 22 is not a whole 2 — check that 22 × 2 does not equal 48.
96 doubles 48 instead of halving it; a 96-tooth gear would rotate only half a turn per pedal rotation.
A 16-tooth gear gives 48 ÷ 16 = 3 rotations, not 2.
hints: You need teeth × 2 rotations = 48 teeth of chain.
So the tooth count is 48 divided by 2.

extending.stem: How would the distance traveled differ with a smaller front wheel on the Penny Farthing? Use the 1 to 1 pedal ratio in your answer.
extending.modelAnswer: The pedal-to-wheel ratio stays 1 to 1, so each pedal rotation still gives exactly one wheel rotation. But a smaller wheel has a shorter perimeter, so each rotation rolls the bike a shorter distance — the rider would have to pedal many more times to go the same distance.
sentenceStems: The ratio stays 1 to 1, but each rotation covers ___ .
So the rider would have to ___ .

extending.stem: How did math help the bicycle's designers come up with ingenious solutions — first with the Penny Farthing, then with chains and gears?
extending.modelAnswer: The Penny Farthing used the math of perimeter: a bigger wheel means more distance per pedal rotation. Gears improved on it with ratios: by choosing 32-tooth or 12-tooth gears against a 48-tooth pedal gear, riders can pick 1.5 or 4 wheel rotations per pedal rotation, trading distance for easier pedaling. Math let designers improve and enhance the solution instead of just making wheels bigger.
sentenceStems: The Penny Farthing used the math of ___ .

practice.commonMistake: Thinking a rear gear with MORE teeth makes the wheel spin more — it is the opposite: the 32-tooth gear gives only 1.5 rotations per pedal rotation, while the 12-tooth gear gives 4.

exitTicket.stem: Which statement best captures what this lesson means by 'Math is Ingenuity'?
choices: Math can help us come up with creative solutions to everyday problems
Math is only useful for inventors who lived in the 1800s
Ingenuity means avoiding math and just guessing
Every bicycle must have a 1 to 1 pedal ratio
exitTicket.explanation: From the Penny Farthing's giant wheel to gear ratios, math powered each creative improvement — that is the lesson's summary.
hints: Look back at the Summarize slide.
It is about creative solutions to everyday problems.
Which option says math helps us create them?

questions.stem: In the Tower of Hanoi, what is the fewest moves needed for 3 disks?
questions.explanation: Three disks take 7 moves. Each extra disk roughly doubles the job.

questions.stem: Look at the pattern 1, 3, 7, 15. What is the rule?
choices: Add the two terms before it

questions.stem: What is the next term in 1, 3, 7, 15, ___?
If 3 disks take 7 moves, how many moves do 4 disks take?
questions.explanation: Move the top 3 disks (7), move the biggest disk (1), then move the 3 back (7): 7 + 1 + 7 = 15.
